metadata.title: An Ogilvy Lens on Accessibility Monitor — Kanishk
metadata.ogilvy_note: Food for thought — not a grade. Ogilvy is one lens among several, running alongside the course rubric. The maker decides.

beats.narration_text: Kanishk's Accessibility Monitor pitch. The smoke detector for your website's accessibility — it watches every deploy, not just the one audit you ran last quarter. The product is working. What would David Ogilvy ask about it?

props.command: I just watched Kanishk's Accessibility Monitor pitch — the smoke detector for your website's accessibility. It watches every deploy and answers: did this release make accessibility better or worse than last time? The pipeline is already working. What do David Ogilvy's principles say about how this pitch frames the work? Not a score. Just the questions a great ad man would ask.

beats.role_note: Show Slide 1, rebuild. 'Smoke detector' is a strong concrete analogy — earns its place. Ogilvy would push it further.
beats.narration_text: Slide 1 — the tagline. Accessibility Monitor: the smoke detector for your website's accessibility. That is a strong concrete analogy. Ogilvy loved physical metaphors over abstract category names. A smoke detector does not scan the room once — it stays on. This one promises the same. The question Ogilvy would ask: what burns down when it fails? The answer to that is the headline this slide is reaching for.

beats.act: LENS 1 — The Person Behind the Number
beats.role_note: Show Slide 2 (problem), rebuild. 96% / 4000 lawsuits / 1-in-4 — great stats, but Ogilvy wants the person.
beats.narration_text: Slide 2 — the problem. Ninety-six percent of websites fail WCAG. Four thousand accessibility lawsuits per year. One in four adults has a disability. Those are real numbers. Ogilvy would stop here and ask: where is the person? Statistics are the shape of a problem — the person is the problem. Who is the blind user who finds the broken alt-text three days after the deploy? That slide would land harder than this one.

beats.act: LENS 2 — The Buried Lead: A Working Pipeline
beats.role_note: Show Slide 9 (POC), rebuild. 'Not a slide-ware idea' is the most powerful fact — on Slide 9.
beats.narration_text: Slide 9 — proof of concept. And here is the line: a working, accountable pipeline — not a slide-ware idea. Ogilvy's second most powerful word, after free, is now. This pipeline runs. Anyone watching this could request access today. The question worth sitting with: the live product is on Slide 9. What if it opened the pitch?

beats.role_note: Show Slide 7 (competition), rebuild. 'No one guards the diff' is the nine-word pitch — on Slide 7.
beats.narration_text: Slide 7 — competition. The headline is: everyone audits a moment in time. No one guards the diff for small teams. That is nine words. It names the mechanism — the diff — it names the gap, and it names the customer. Ogilvy: a specific competitive claim always outperforms a general one. This one earns its place. The question is whether it stays here on Slide 7 or whether it leads.

beats.act: LENS 4 — Free Is the Most Powerful Word
beats.role_note: No slide needed. Free tier + live product = the unstated strongest ask.
beats.narration_text: There is a free tier. Zero dollars, first accessibility scan, no setup required. Ogilvy was explicit: free is the most powerful word in advertising. The product is live. The free tier exists. The ask slide requests design partners and technical help — both useful. But the most direct ask in this pitch is the one not stated: go run your first diff today. Why is that not the last line?

beats.act: LENS 5 — The Close: The Last Line Is the Strongest
beats.role_note: Show Slide 10 (ask), rebuild. The closing quote is the strongest line in the pitch.
beats.narration_text: Slide 10 — the ask. Design partners, technical help, seed support. Standard and right-sized for an early-stage product. But then there is the closing line: accessibility burns down in the dark — no one smells the smoke until someone is harmed. Ogilvy: a close should end on something the audience carries out of the room. That line does it. The question is whether the ask lives up to it.

beats.role_note: Not a verdict: four questions for the next draft.
beats.narration_text: Not a verdict — a lens set. Four questions for the next draft. One: the smoke detector analogy is specific — what burns when it fails? Two: ninety-six percent is a statistic — who is the person? Three: 'no one guards the diff' is nine words and the whole pitch — why is it on Slide 7? Four: free tier, live product — why not end with 'run your first diff today'? These are Ogilvy's questions. The pitch decides which ones matter.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take your deck into Claude and try this: here are four Ogilvy questions about my pitch. For each one — which specific slide is most in play, and what is one alternative frame to consider? Not a correction, just another angle. The goal is not to score the pitch. Ogilvy is one lens. The course rubric is another.
